text.p: The Belgian parliament approved early on Friday the government's 1997 budget after a debate dominated by opposition allegations that the Finance Ministry had recklessly speculated on financial markets in the early 1990s to reduce Belgium's debt.

The budget, presented on Tuesday, aims to reduce the public sector deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from a forecast 3.3 percent in 1996, and to secure Belgium's place in European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The confidence vote, won by 81 to 58 votes by the centre-left coalition, was a formality after the government earlier this year was given special powers to push through the budget by decree if necessary.

The government says the 80 billion Belgian franc deficit reduction package will clear the way for Belgium's entry into the final stage of economic and monetary union in Europe, due to start in 1999, since it will push the deficit/GDP ratio down to below the level required in the Maastricht Treaty on EMU.
The two-and-a-half day budget debate was dominated by surprise opposition allegations that the 1989-1992 government led by Wilfried Martens had secretly speculated on the foreign exchange market.
Swap positions built up now threatened to cost the state 44 billion Belgian francs, the opposition said.

Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said that if all of the current transactions, due between 1997 and 2002, were terminated early, under today's market conditions the net result would be a loss of 34 billion francs.
But Maystadt, who also was finance minister in the Martens government, said it was too early to say what the budget impact would be when the contracts expire at the envisaged dates.
